about: The world's ancient sites on one great circle, as the claim's own author draws it: Jim Alison's table of sites near the circle, in his figures (degrees and minutes as he prints them; his distance off the circle in statute miles, rounded as he rounds it). These are what the proponent says, like a text's figures: never measurements, verified false until read again on the page. The circle itself is not stored; the exhibit fits it from these coordinates and compares the fit with the axis he gives. Each site's own coordinates and dates, from its own source, are a later step. Each site's "own" block is the same place as an encyclopedia gives it, read 2026-10-21 (chunk 12): its point and the years of the work the circle is said to pass (built, carved, occupied, as "what" says), BCE negative and no year zero, with the article's words in "reading" and null where the source gives no year or the site is no work at all.

axis.note: The circle's northern axis point as the page gives it, 'in northwestern British Columbia'; the southern one is its antipode, 59 53 S, 41 24 E.

tolerances: within one tenth of one degree of this great circle (Giza, Tassili n'Ajjer, Paratoari, Ollantaytambo, Nazca, Easter Island and others, as the page lists them)
within one quarter of a degree (Machupicchu and Cuzco; Siwa; Mohenjo Daro and Ganweriwala; Preah Vihear)
within one degree of the great circle (Ur and Angkor)
